"kill" is the slightly unfortunate name given to the command to send a signal to a process. Signals are a way for linux to interrupt a process for various reasons, like tell it to do something. Many different signals exist, and they each have a number. If the process has a signal handler for that specific signal, the program code in that handler will be run by the process. Otherwise, a default action will be taken. There is no way to handle or block SIGKILL though, it always just terminates the process. SIGKILL is the signal with code 9, that's why kill -9 sends it.

Read more about signals here
And here's a list of all signals

EDIT: To answer your original question, the default signal for the kill command, when you just do kill <pid> seems to be 15, SIGTERM, which makes sense because what this does is allow the process to quickly clean up resources and terminate itself if it cares to. Of course this may not always work, like if the process is misbehaved, or if was the middle of a sensitive action, it may have temporarily blocked the signal, waiting for it to be delivered later.

TL;DR: Try kill <pid>, and if that doesn't work, do kill -9 <pid>

Command breakdown:

  • find is the command that finds things (duh)
  • . is the name of the directory whose contents including subdirectories you want to search. So, if you want to check the entire system, you'd replace this with /. To check your home directory, replace it with ~ or $HOME.

  • -name "*firefox*" tells it that the name should have firefox in it and the two *s tell it that it's okay to have other stuff in the name before and after firefox (but it must have firefox). If you know the exact name is firefox, you don't need the quotes, just use -name firefox.

This isn't the best way to go about it, in my opinion. Why are these commands named what they are? What does "ps" stand for? Why are the switches what they are? -C is uppercase; why not lowercase and what does it do with or without that switch? Ditto the -9.

Windows Powershell would be things like Get-Process. There are standardized verb-noun pairs and the switches are logical things like -Path, -Parameters, -NoOutput, etc (none case-sensitive, btw). You also have a single place on the internet to search for how they work and how they interact (TechNet).

Most of the nomenclature was developed during a time wherein you had to deal with very slow access to the terminal, particularly if you were using a modem. Typing 'cp -a fileA fileB' could make a real difference compared to 'copy /allattribs fileA fileB', for instance. The fact that it saved a few bytes of memory when main memory sizes usually measured in KB didn't hurt, either. Many commands that followed on after it kept a similar nomenclature.

'ps' stands for 'ProccesS', if I recall correctly. -9 is the name of a specific signal you're sending, and I think most commands that use it in modern distros will also accept it by its human-readable name, SIGKILL, which basically tells the OS to shoot it down. Case matters because in many cases, command-line programs are so feature-rich that they run out of shorthand names for switches, so sometimes they need to double up (e.g. -C and -c). Command line programs in Unix, at least according to the traditional scheme, are intended to be capable of being strung together so that you can do a very large variety of tasks with simple, reliable components and slap it together without much effort on the fly. Most people who are going to be using Mint for the first time are not going to be in a position to appreciate this, unfortunately, but they can still use most of the basic commands without much difficulty. These are often things that are fundamentally difficult to do well with a GUI given a lack of flexibility, which is a fact often lost on people who are Microsoft devotees (at least, until they experience them themselves). In fact, this sort of thing is one of the main reasons PowerShell exists in the first place.

Linux command-line programs are usually documented by their manual pages, which are built-in to the actual system you're working with (no need for TechNet with those). To use them, type:

man commandname

While it is true that Microsoft's Technet is a single place to look for it on the Internet, PowerShell is also controlled by one company, has not been around for decades to get the bugs hammered out and build a culture around it, and is brought to you by the same people who think giving away spyware as an operating system is a good idea. Additionally it also ensures you will not have alternate opinions, or the possibility of fixes for problems in other places.

File management is a pretty basic and necessary skill:

Many commands operate relative to your current "working directory". To print your current working directory:

pwd

To list all the files and directories in your working directory:

ls

To list the contents of another directory:

ls <name of dir>

To change your working directory:

cd <name of dir>

There are some special directories:

'.' (a period): means your current working directory

'..' (two periods): means the directory above your current one (the one your current directory is inside of)

'~' (tilde): your home directory, where all of your personal files go by default

'/' (forward slash): root; the top; every file and directory on the system is inside root

To delete a file:

rm <name of file>

To delete an empty directory:

rmdir <name of dir>

To delete a non-empty directory (careful!):

rm -r <name of dir>

IF A COMMAND INVOLVES ANYTHING THAT SAYS /dev/ BE ABSOLUTELY CERTAIN YOU ARE DOING IT RIGHT. DO NOT TAKE CHANCES. IF YOU ARE NOT CERTAIN, DO NOT DO IT UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES.

The problem with Linux is that Adobe, AvID protools, Autodesk's Maya, and Blackmagic Davinci Resolve won't run on the platform. Nor Microsoft Office. You can't use industry standard tools to write, storyboard, edit, animate and composite, color correct, and encode for broadcast or printing.

But you can do these things.

Blender is an all around tool that is a good 3D modeler, a good puppet rigging tool, and a rather slow rendering system. But it does produce professional quality output. It also includes a non-linear editor and compositing system that rivals After Effects. It can be used for 2D animations quite readily. And what about color correction? There's a even two wheel RGB color editor in Blender. Davinci kicks its ass. But you can do basic color correction. Blender is really a Swiss army knife of film for Linux.

GIMP is a piece of shit. It can't even handle layer masks. But you need a photo editing tool. Krita does handle layer masks and more. But it's a QT program. Don't you just love the old 90s Gnome/KDE wars leaving cruft all over your system twenty years later? Yeah, well get used to it. Because Krita kicks GIMP's ass. About the only thing GIMP is useful for is automation through script-fu. Which can be called from Blender with Python scripting. So if there's a GIMP module you want to use in Blender, that's possible. And could well be useful. Definitely install GIMP too.

Inkscape. Vector editing program. Nowhere near as good as Adobe Illustrator. And it slows down badly the bigger your project gets. BUT, if used judiciously you can integrate your workflow from here to Blender for good quality 2D animations. A must have.

The latest LibreOffice 3.0. This is actually really good. I'm impressed. There's no screenplay macros out that I know of. But really, learn the damn format and do it by hand.

You won't get a job doing it this way. But you could write, storyboard, shoot, edit, add composite art like titling and even 3D motion effects, color correct, and finally even print a semi-professional film (on stock or digitally). With entirely free software.

Linux user here since '97, cross-platform developer supporting users that use both platforms for most of last 2 decades. Here's a few observations based on my experience:

  • It's an alien concept to new Linux users that Linux can look different. Windows is the way it is because GUI and OS are inseparable. One of the first things I explain is that Linux offers many Desktops to choose from based on what you like. That default look, and tools for managing installed software and system configuration, are the chief things that make Linux distributions different from each other. Pick one you like and understand that you can change almost anything later as you learn. I personally recommend a KDE-based distro for a more familiar transition: Kubuntu if they've got nice, modern hardware because so much "just works" or Linux Mint KDE on older boxes because it's relatively lightweight.

Avoid telling them volatile things like key shortcuts to memorize -- that's only going to add to the confusion if their chosen Desktop differs from yours and the can of worms opened in explanation isn't going to sooth any transition nerves.

  • The Linux Documentation Project, TLDP, is dated but still an excellent free resource. There are some things a new user needs to be aware of about what's going on under the hood that's philosophically different from Windows. Aware, not necessarily an instant expert. My recommened skimming list, in order of priority, is as follows:
  • Disk directory layout whats & whys -- The Linux File System Hierarchical Standard. At least skim this so as not to be lost and baffled.

  • Basics of system administration on a Un*x-family box -- The Linux System Administrators Guide. Very dated with respect to modern GUIs but the core concepts are there. Users, Groups, and directory permissions are essential to understand right out of the gate. Differences in PATH behavior and what makes a file/script executable are also core points of difference that can lead to frustration.

  • Make them aware of core applications, like Libre Office and GIMP, a good media player (VLC or Dragon or Amarok), a good disc burner (K3B), and help them activate DVD playback (the whole DeCSS DMCA discussion can best be had later)

  • Show them how to use the Package Manager for their chosen distro to browse/add new software. This is a good time for a quick mention of the differing philosophies of Windows versus Linux software distribution -- unverifiable binaries downloadable from random websites versus signed packages from trusted repositories (kind of like an app store, that even Microsoft is trying to shift towards).

  • Lastly, mention that if they purchase higher-end hardware or do a little research online first, most hardware is just detected and supported by Linux automatically and there's no need for the almighty Driver Disk.

This is a tried and true pathway I've led quite a number of folks down. Linux is not difficult but there are very basic differences that can frustrate and intimidate even technically-savvy users when they've simply just never encountered a particular way of thinking before. Guide them over the conceptual differences and commands and keypresses will fall into place.
